1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: The patient is a 66-year-old woman who was admitted on Day 0 with the chief complaint of "recurrent cough, sputum production, and shortness of breath for more than 5 months." In approximately 6 months before Day 0, after caring for a family member with fever, she developed cough, sputum production, and shortness of breath. In early October, she presented to a local hospital, where contrast-enhanced chest CT showed: 1. Multiple patchy mass-like and nodular high-density lesions in both lungs, with special infection considered highly likely, although differentiation from neoplastic lesions was still needed; 2. Multiple mildly enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes; 3. Small bilateral pleural effusions. Outside hospital tests showed elevated WBC, elevated neutrophil percentage, elevated CRP, and normal PCT. Tumor markers: cytokeratin 19 fragment 4.130 ng/ml, CA125 65.1 U/ml, CA19-9 32.7 U/ml, ferritin 1390 μg/L. Rheumatologic markers were negative. PET/CT showed localized inflammation in the left maxillary alveolar region; multiple patchy, mass-like, and nodular lesions in both lungs with varying degrees of increased metabolism, with special infection considered possible. Bronchoscopy TNGS indicated Candida albicans, among others. Send-out BALF GM and Cryptococcus were both negative. Sputum culture: Enterobacteriaceae and Candida albicans 1+. Transbronchial needle biopsy of the right middle lobe on bronchoscopy showed no tumor; the diagnosis was considered to be Candida pneumonia, among others. After anti-infective and anti-inflammatory treatment, symptom relief was not obvious, and repeat chest CT showed progression of the bilateral pulmonary lesions compared with before. Past history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, apical periodontitis of the right maxillary third molar, hepatitis B, among others. Physical examination on admission: enlarged right submandibular lymph node palpable; scattered moist rales audible in both lungs. Preliminary diagnosis: multiple pulmonary lesions of undetermined nature, special infection? tumor? etc. Repeat sinus + chest CT on admission showed: 1. Mild bilateral maxillary sinus inflammation. 2. Consider lung cancer in the anteromedial basal segment of the left upper lobe with multiple metastases to both lungs and pleura, and hilar and mediastinal lymph node metastases. 3. Small left pleural effusion.

stage2_input.text: After admission, laboratory and other examinations were completed: CBC showed persistently elevated WBC and neutrophil percentage, mildly elevated PCT, and elevated ESR and CRP. G test, two-item fungal antigen test, sputum smear, sputum culture, BALF culture, and BALF-Mycobacterium tuberculosis nucleic acid test were negative. BALF DNA mNGS and DNA+RNA mNGS of left percutaneous transthoracic lung tissue were both negative. Five lung tumor markers: neuron-specific enolase 19.50 ng/ml, CA125 131 U/ml. Immune panel of eight items and TBNK cell testing showed no obvious immunodeficiency. Rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, 11-item antinuclear antibody profile, autoimmune myositis antibody profile, and five-item vasculitis panel were all negative. Induced sputum and BALF cytologic differential were both predominantly neutrophils. Bronchoscopic lymph node needle aspiration biopsy showed no tumor cells. Breast ultrasound showed a hypoechoic nodule in the left breast and multiple enlarged bilateral axillary lymph nodes. Cervical lymph node ultrasound showed multiple enlarged bilateral subcutaneous cervical lymph nodes.

recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has had recurrent cough, sputum production, and dyspnea for more than 5 months. Multiple mass-like, nodular, and consolidation-like lesions in both lungs have shown persistent progression, accompanied by mediastinal/hilar and multiple systemic lymphadenopathy, a small pleural effusion, and weight loss. Previous multiple bronchoscopies, lung biopsies, and EBUS-guided needle aspirations did not yield evidence of tumor. Antibacterial therapy, antifungal therapy, and short-term corticosteroid treatment were all ineffective. Routine pathogen testing, BALF, and tissue mNGS also did not identify a definite cause, suggesting that infection or inflammation alone is insufficient to explain the findings, while routine sampling also has sampling limitations. A prior PET/CT showed increased metabolic activity in the bilateral pulmonary lesions but still favored atypical infection. Clinically, further molecular imaging, which is more helpful for localization and characterization of systemic lesions, is needed to reassess the extent of systemic involvement, identify the most representative as well as the safest and most efficient biopsy target, and help distinguish among malignant tumor, malignant lymphoma, and inflammatory lesions. This examination plays a key role in clarifying the etiology, performing staging assessment, and guiding the next puncture pathway and subsequent treatment strategy selection.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: The pathology report from the patient's right maxillofacial biopsy on Day +17 showed B-cell lymphoma, favoring diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: In the context of a prolonged disease course, progressively increasing and enlarging pulmonary lesions, multistation systemic lymphadenopathy, and the inability of multiple prior small lung and mediastinal specimens to establish a definitive diagnosis, FAPI-PET-CT identified a hypermetabolic mass in the right inferior temporal/maxillofacial region, representing a new lesion site that was highly suspicious on imaging and relatively accessible. Biopsy with pathologic evaluation of this site was chosen because a more intact tissue architecture was needed to determine whether lymphoma or another malignant tumor was present, thereby compensating for the limited diagnostic capability of small lung specimens for nonepithelial tumors. The core purpose of this examination was to obtain final histologic evidence, clarify the pathologic type, and use pathology and immunophenotype to distinguish malignant lymphoma from metastatic carcinoma, chronic infectious granuloma, or reactive hyperplasia. The result directly affected the final confirmed diagnosis, disease classification, and the subsequent decision to transfer to Hematology for treatment with regimens such as R-CHOP.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Bone marrow aspiration result: no tumor identified.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The final pathology has indicated B-cell lymphoma, favoring diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, while imaging shows extensive bilateral pulmonary lesions and multistation lymph node involvement in the bilateral neck, hilar, mediastinal, axillary, and internal mammary regions, suggesting possible systemic disease. At this time, the main purpose of bone marrow aspiration was not initial etiologic screening, but to assess whether the bone marrow was involved, to complete lymphoma staging and tumor burden assessment, and to comprehensively evaluate the extent of disease together with the multiple pulmonary lesions and systemic lymph node involvement. Bone marrow examination can also help exclude hematologic involvement caused by bone marrow infiltration, providing a basis for subsequent treatment intensity selection, prognostic assessment, and baseline evaluation before chemotherapy. No tumor was seen in the bone marrow aspiration result, which has important reference value for staging assessment and treatment planning.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: After hospital-wide MDT discussion, it was recommended to repeat FAPI-PET-CT to further clarify the etiology. On Day +11, repeat whole-body FAPI-PET-CT showed: 1. A mass lesion with high FAP uptake in the inferior right temporal region, considered likely a malignant tumor (malignant mesenchymal tumor? malignant lymphoma?); PET/CT-guided needle biopsy by the Department of Nuclear Medicine molecular imaging was recommended. 2. Multiple nodules, patchy opacities, and mass-like consolidative lesions in all lobes of both lungs, with markedly increased FAPI uptake; compared with the prior outside-hospital PET/CT, the number had increased and the extent had enlarged, considered likely multiple pulmonary metastases. 3. Multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral neck (levels I and II), bilateral hila, mediastinum, bilateral axillae, left internal mammary region, and cardiophrenic angle region, some with increased FAPI uptake, considered likely multiple lymph node metastases. The pathology report from the right maxillofacial biopsy on Day +17 showed: B-cell lymphoma, favor diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Bone marrow aspiration result: no tumor seen.

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; lymphoma involving the skin and lungs
diagnostic_basis: Elderly female, subacute onset, chest CT showed multiple bilateral quasi-spherical and consolidative lesions; poor response to anti-infective therapy.

Whole-body FAPI-PET-CT showed a right inferotemporal FAP-avid mass, multiple nodules, patchy and mass-like areas of consolidation in all lobes of both lungs, and multiple enlarged lymph nodes; pathology from a right maxillofacial biopsy: B-cell lymphoma, favor diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

treatment_plan: Transferred to the Hematology Department for further treatment
treated with 4 cycles of the R-CHOP regimen
treatment_response: After 3 cycles of treatment, repeat chest CT showed marked resolution of the lesions compared with prior imaging, and the cough symptoms improved significantly.
On follow-up, the lesions were significantly smaller than before, and the severe cough that had troubled the patient the most was also markedly relieved.
